title: Low Tolerance for Alcohol: Why You Get Drunk So Easily
excerpt: Why do you get drunk so easily? The real reasons behind a low tolerance for alcohol, why it can drop suddenly, when it's worth seeing a doctor, and how to drink comfortably with it.
metaDescription: Why do you get drunk so easily? The real causes of low alcohol tolerance, why it can drop suddenly, when to see a doctor, and how to drink comfortably.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: why do i get drunk so easily
content:
**The honest answer first:** if you get drunk on one or two drinks, the cause is almost always ordinary biology rather than something wrong with you. How fast alcohol reaches your blood, how much water your body has to dilute it, how quickly your liver clears it, and how used to it your brain is all vary a lot from person to person. Body size, sex, food, sleep, genes, medications, and how often you drink explain most low tolerance. A sudden, unexplained drop in tolerance is the one situation that deserves a closer look, and a few warning signs mean you should get medical help right away.

**The quick version:** smaller bodies, less body water, an empty stomach, fizzy or strong drinks, little sleep, and drinking rarely all make the same drink hit harder. Some medicines multiply alcohol's effect, and some genetic variants change how your body handles it. Low tolerance isn't a flaw to train away. It means each drink does more, so you need fewer of them, which is mostly good news for your liver, your sleep, and your wallet.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article explains general research. It is not a substitute for a clinician who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist if** your tolerance dropped suddenly without an obvious reason (like a long break, weight loss, or a new medicine), you started a new prescription and now feel much more affected by alcohol, you get hives, wheezing, swelling, or a racing heart after small amounts, you have pain anywhere in your body after drinking, you've had weight-loss surgery, or you keep losing memory of parts of the night after only a few drinks. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if** someone is confused, can't be woken, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and they can happen at lower amounts when alcohol is mixed with sedating medicines.

## What "Low Tolerance for Alcohol" Actually Means

People use "low tolerance" to describe two different experiences, and it helps to separate them.

1. **You reach a high blood alcohol level from fewer drinks.** This is about the physical concentration of alcohol in your blood (your BAC). Two people can drink the same amount and end up with quite different BACs because of body size, body water, food, and how fast their stomach empties.
2. **You feel more impaired at the same blood alcohol level.** This is about how your brain responds. Someone who drinks often develops what researchers call functional tolerance: the brain adapts and the person looks and feels less drunk at a given BAC, even though the alcohol in their blood is just as high.

Most people with a low tolerance have a bit of both. They reach a higher BAC per drink *and* their brain isn't adapted, so they feel it strongly. If you want the full picture of how tolerance builds and fades, our guide to [alcohol tolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-tolerance) covers the different types in more detail. This page focuses on the practical question most people are really asking: **why do I get drunk so easily, and is that normal?**

It's also worth separating low tolerance from **alcohol intolerance**. Intolerance is a reaction to alcohol or to something in the drink, such as flushing, a stuffy nose, hives, headache, or nausea after a small amount. You can have low tolerance without intolerance, intolerance without low tolerance, or both. We cover the reaction side in our [alcohol intolerance guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance).

## How Alcohol Gets From Your Glass to Your Brain

To understand why the same drink hits people differently, it helps to know the basic path alcohol takes.

- **Stomach.** A small amount of alcohol is absorbed here, and a little is broken down by an enzyme in the stomach lining before it ever reaches the blood. While the stomach holds the drink, absorption is slow.
- **Small intestine.** Most alcohol is absorbed here, and fast. Anything that speeds the trip from stomach to intestine, like an empty stomach or a carbonated mixer, sends alcohol into your blood faster and produces a higher, sharper peak.
- **Bloodstream and body water.** Alcohol spreads through the water in your body. It doesn't dissolve well in fat. The more water your body holds, the more diluted each drink becomes.
- **Liver.** The liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for an average adult, though this varies. It first turns alcohol into acetaldehyde (a toxic compound) and then into harmless acetate. You can read more about this in [how alcohol is metabolized](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-is-metabolized).
- **Brain.** Alcohol boosts the brain's main calming signal (GABA) and dampens its main excitatory signal (glutamate). That's what causes relaxation at first, then slowed reactions, poor coordination, and eventually memory gaps.

Every factor below acts on one or more of these steps.

## The Main Reasons You Get Drunk Easily

### 1. Body size

This is the simplest one. A drink delivers a fixed amount of alcohol, and a smaller body has less blood and water to spread it through. A person who weighs 120 pounds will usually reach a noticeably higher BAC from the same glass of wine than a person who weighs 200 pounds. Standard BAC estimates (like the Widmark formula used in many online calculators) are built around this relationship.

### 2. Body composition and body water

Two people of the same weight can still differ. Muscle holds a lot of water, and fat holds very little. Since alcohol stays mostly in the body's water, someone with a higher proportion of body fat has less water to dilute it and tends to reach a higher BAC. This is one reason tolerance can feel lower after losing muscle, during illness, or as you get older.

### 3. Sex

On average, women reach higher BACs than men after the same amount of alcohol, even at the same body weight. Three things contribute. Women tend to have a lower proportion of body water. Research published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* in 1990 (Frezza and colleagues) found that women, on average, broke down less alcohol in the stomach before it reached the blood. And hormonal shifts across the menstrual cycle may affect how alcohol feels, although studies on that point are mixed. This is why official drinking guidelines in the US and elsewhere set lower limits for women.

### 4. An empty stomach

Drinking without food is one of the most common reasons people say "it hit me out of nowhere." With nothing in the stomach, the valve between the stomach and small intestine opens quickly and alcohol rushes to the place where it's absorbed fastest. Food, especially a meal with protein, fat, and fiber, keeps the drink in the stomach longer, so alcohol trickles into the blood more slowly and the peak is lower. Our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) goes through this in more detail.

### 5. What you're drinking and how fast

- **Stronger drinks.** A cocktail can contain two or more standard drinks. Craft beers at 8 to 10 percent alcohol, a generous restaurant wine pour, or a heavy-handed home pour can each count as more than one drink.
- **Fizzy drinks.** Carbonation appears to speed stomach emptying for many people. Small studies have found that alcohol mixed with carbonated water produced a faster rise in BAC than the same alcohol mixed with still water, though not everyone responds the same way. Champagne, hard seltzers, and spirits with soda are the usual suspects.
- **Diet mixers.** Some small studies have reported higher BACs when spirits were mixed with diet soda rather than regular soda, possibly because sugar slows stomach emptying a little. The effect is real enough to be worth knowing about, but the research is limited.
- **Speed.** Your liver clears alcohol at a steady pace no matter how fast you drink. Three drinks in an hour produce a much higher peak than three drinks across an evening.

If "how many drinks is it?" is the part you're unsure about, our guide to [how many drinks it takes to get drunk](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-to-get-drunk) explains standard drink sizes.

### 6. You don't drink very often

This is the biggest reason for low tolerance in people who are otherwise average in size. When you drink regularly, your brain adapts to alcohol's calming effect and your liver ramps up a backup enzyme system (called CYP2E1) that helps clear alcohol a bit faster. When you drink rarely, neither adaptation is there. The result: you feel more from each drink. People often notice this after a dry month, pregnancy, illness, or simply a period of drinking less.

This is not a problem to fix. A tolerance that rises is the body adapting to regular alcohol exposure, and higher tolerance is linked with drinking more, which raises long-term health risks. A tolerance that's low means you get the effect you want from less.

### 7. Not enough sleep

Being tired and drinking stack on top of each other. Both slow reaction time and impair judgment, and studies on sleep deprivation and alcohol have found that the combination impairs driving performance more than either one alone. If you've had a short night or a long week, the same two drinks can feel like four.

### 8. Dehydration, heat, and exercise

Being dehydrated doesn't change your BAC very much on its own, but it can make you feel worse: lightheaded, headachy, and wiped out. Drinking in the sun, after a workout, or after a long flight can make modest amounts feel stronger than usual. Altitude is a common example. Research suggests altitude itself doesn't change BAC much, but the combination of mild dehydration, poor sleep, and low oxygen can make people feel more affected.

### 9. Age

Many people say their tolerance drops in their 40s, 50s, and beyond. Several changes add up: the body's proportion of water falls and muscle mass declines, the liver may clear alcohol a bit more slowly, people tend to take more medications, and the aging brain can be more sensitive to alcohol's effects on balance and memory. This is also part of why [hangovers tend to feel worse with age](/never-hungover/why-hangovers-get-worse-with-age).

### 10. Genetics

Your genes shape how you process alcohol, and the effects show up in two main ways.

- **ALDH2 variants.** A common variant in the ALDH2 gene, found in many people of East Asian descent, slows the breakdown of acetaldehyde. Acetaldehyde builds up and causes facial flushing, a fast heartbeat, nausea, and headaches after small amounts. This is often called Asian flush, and it's covered in our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive). People with this variant often feel unwell quickly, which they may describe as low tolerance. It also raises the risk of esophageal cancer for people who keep drinking despite the reaction, so the flush is a signal worth respecting.
- **ADH1B variants.** Some people carry a version of the ADH1B gene that converts alcohol to acetaldehyde faster. This can also lead to discomfort after small amounts.
- **Brain sensitivity.** Beyond enzymes, research on family history and alcohol response suggests that people vary in how strongly their brain reacts to alcohol. Interestingly, studies led by Marc Schuckit found that people who feel *less* effect from alcohol early in life were more likely to develop drinking problems later. Feeling alcohol strongly is, if anything, a protective trait.

### 11. Medications

This is the cause most worth taking seriously. Many common medicines add to alcohol's sedating effect, and some interfere with how it's broken down. Examples include:

- **Sleep aids and anxiety medicines**, such as benzodiazepines and prescription sleep pills.
- **Opioid pain medicines.**
- **Sedating antihistamines**, like diphenhydramine (found in many allergy and nighttime products) and doxylamine.
- **Some antidepressants and antipsychotics.**
- **Nerve-pain and seizure medicines** such as gabapentin and pregabalin.
- **Muscle relaxants.**
- **Some antibiotics and antifungals.** Metronidazole and tinidazole can cause a severe reaction with alcohol, and labels tell you to avoid alcohol while taking them and for a few days after.

The combination can do more than make you feel drunk faster. Sedating medicines plus alcohol can slow breathing, which is dangerous. If you started a new prescription and noticed your tolerance changed, read the label, ask your pharmacist, and don't assume small amounts are safe. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) also covers what to check before combining any supplement with medication.

### 12. Health conditions

Some health conditions change how alcohol affects you:

- **Weight-loss surgery.** Gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy change how quickly alcohol leaves the stomach. Studies have found that people who've had these surgeries reach higher BAC peaks, faster, after the same drink. Some research has also linked gastric bypass with a higher risk of developing alcohol problems later, so it's worth discussing with your surgical team.
- **Liver disease.** A liver that's struggling clears alcohol more slowly and is more vulnerable to damage from it.
- **Diabetes and low blood sugar.** Alcohol can lower blood sugar, and the symptoms of low blood sugar (shakiness, confusion, sweating) can look a lot like being drunk.
- **Recent illness.** After a stomach bug, flu, or COVID, many people notice they feel alcohol more for a while. Reduced eating, dehydration, and fatigue probably all play a part.

### 13. Your mood and setting

Expectations and setting matter more than people think. Stress, anxiety, and an empty or tired body can all make alcohol feel stronger. In some studies, people who expected to be drunk acted more impaired even when given a placebo drink. That doesn't mean your low tolerance is "in your head," but it does mean context shifts how a drink feels.

## Why Do I Get Drunk So Easily All of a Sudden?

If your tolerance changed recently, run through this checklist. Most sudden changes have an ordinary explanation.

- **You've been drinking less.** Even a few weeks off can noticeably lower tolerance.
- **You lost weight**, especially muscle, or changed your diet a lot (for example, a low-carb diet or long fasting windows).
- **You started a new medicine**, including over-the-counter allergy or sleep products. Some newer weight-loss and diabetes medicines slow stomach emptying, and people taking them sometimes report that alcohol feels different. The research is still early, so ask your prescriber how alcohol fits with your treatment.
- **You're sleeping badly or under a lot of stress.**
- **You've changed drinks**, such as switching from light beer to craft beer or cocktails.
- **You're older than you were** the last time you drank regularly.
- **You've been ill** recently.
- **You've had surgery**, especially on the stomach.
- **Hormonal changes**, including pregnancy, the postpartum period, or perimenopause.

If none of these fit and you feel very affected by small amounts, or if the change came with other symptoms like fatigue, weight loss, yellowing of the skin or eyes, abdominal swelling, or easy bruising, see a doctor. These can be signs of liver trouble or another condition that's worth checking.

## Is Low Alcohol Tolerance a Bad Sign?

Usually not. For most people, low tolerance simply reflects a smaller body, light or occasional drinking, or one of the ordinary factors above. Feeling alcohol strongly is not a sign of liver damage in itself.

The situations where it's worth paying attention are:

- **A sudden change** with no explanation from the checklist above.
- **Reactions rather than intoxication**, such as hives, wheezing, swelling, severe flushing, or a pounding heart after a sip or two. These point toward intolerance or, rarely, allergy.
- **Pain after drinking.** Pain in the lymph nodes, chest, or abdomen after small amounts of alcohol is uncommon and should be checked by a doctor.
- **Memory gaps after small amounts.** If you're blacking out after only a few drinks, especially with medications involved, talk to a doctor. Our guide to [blackouts](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk) explains what's happening in the brain.

## Should You Try to Raise Your Tolerance?

No, and this is worth being direct about. Building tolerance means drinking more often or in larger amounts so your brain and liver adapt. That adaptation doesn't protect your body. Your liver, heart, gut, and brain are still exposed to the full amount of alcohol, and you need more of it to feel the same thing. Higher tolerance is also one of the early signs doctors look for when they assess whether someone's drinking is becoming a problem.

There's also a safety trap. A person with high functional tolerance can look sober while their BAC is well over the legal driving limit, because tolerance doesn't lower the amount of alcohol in the blood. Our explainer on [what BAC is](/never-hungover/what-is-bac) covers this.

A low tolerance is a good deal: you get the relaxed, social feeling from fewer drinks. The goal is to work *with* it, not against it.

## How to Drink Comfortably With a Low Tolerance

These are practical ways to avoid getting drunker than you meant to.

1. **Eat a real meal first.** Protein, fat, and fiber slow absorption. Keep snacking through the evening.
2. **Know your drink sizes.** In the US, one standard drink is about 12 ounces of 5 percent beer, 5 ounces of 12 percent wine, or 1.5 ounces of 40 percent spirits. Check the alcohol percentage on beer and seltzer cans.
3. **Pace to roughly one drink per hour or slower.** Set a number before you go out.
4. **Alternate with water or a non-alcoholic drink.** It slows your pace and keeps you hydrated.
5. **Be careful with fizzy drinks and shots.** If carbonated drinks hit you hard, choose still mixers or sip slowly.
6. **Choose lower-strength options.** Session beers, wine spritzers, or a single spirit with plenty of mixer.
7. **Check your medications.** Read labels for alcohol warnings and ask your pharmacist about anything sedating.
8. **Don't drink when you're exhausted.** If you're running on little sleep, have less than usual.
9. **Plan your ride home.** Never rely on how you feel to judge whether you can drive. With a low tolerance, the gap between "feeling fine" and impaired can be small, and with a high tolerance, feeling fine can be misleading.

For more tactics, see our guide on [how to not get drunk](/never-hungover/how-to-not-get-drunk).

## Does Low Tolerance Mean Worse Hangovers?

Not necessarily, but the two often travel together. If you get drunk easily, it's often because your BAC rises higher per drink, and higher peaks tend to bring worse sleep, more dehydration, and more acetaldehyde for your body to clear. People with genetic variants that slow acetaldehyde breakdown also tend to feel worse the next day.

On the other hand, people with low tolerance often drink less overall, which is the most reliable way to avoid a hangover. If you notice you get bad hangovers from small amounts, our guide to [why some people get hangovers so easily](/never-hungover/why-do-i-get-hangovers-so-easily) digs into the reasons.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the brain. In a 2012 study in rats published in the *Journal of Neuroscience* (Shen and colleagues), DHM reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal, apparently by acting on GABA receptors. Other animal research suggests it may support the enzymes that clear alcohol and acetaldehyde. Human evidence is much more limited.

To be clear about what this means for low tolerance:

- **There is no good evidence that DHM raises your tolerance** or lets you drink more safely. It does not lower your BAC in any way you can rely on, and it doesn't make it safe to drive.
- **It's not a substitute** for food, pacing, and checking your medications.
- **Some people take it** before or during a night out as part of a broader plan to feel better the next day, alongside water, food, and sensible limits.

If you want to try it, a well-reviewed single-ingredient option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

Getting drunk easily is usually normal. Body size, body water, sex, food, the strength and fizz of your drinks, how often you drink, sleep, age, genes, and medications explain nearly every case. The most useful thing you can do is work with your tolerance: eat, pace, know your pours, and check your medicines. Don't try to build tolerance up, because that just means more alcohol exposure for the same effect. And pay attention to the exceptions: a sudden unexplained drop, reactions like hives or a pounding heart, pain after drinking, or blackouts after small amounts are reasons to see a doctor. Signs of alcohol poisoning, like confusion, trouble breathing, or being unable to wake someone, need emergency help right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I get drunk so easily?**

Usually because of ordinary biology. A smaller body, less body water, drinking on an empty stomach, strong or fizzy drinks, drinking quickly, poor sleep, and drinking only occasionally all make each drink hit harder. Genetics and some medicines can add to that. If your tolerance dropped suddenly with no clear reason, or you have other symptoms, talk to a doctor.

**Is having a low tolerance for alcohol bad?**

Usually not. Low tolerance means you feel the effects from fewer drinks, which tends to mean less alcohol exposure overall. It's worth checking with a doctor if the change was sudden and unexplained, if you get reactions like hives or a racing heart from small amounts, if drinking causes pain, or if you black out after only a few drinks.

**Why is my alcohol tolerance suddenly so low?**

The most common reasons are drinking less than you used to, losing weight or muscle, starting a new medication, poor sleep or stress, switching to stronger drinks, recent illness, stomach surgery, or hormonal changes. If none of these fit, or you also have fatigue, yellow skin or eyes, or easy bruising, see a doctor.

**Why do women get drunk faster than men?**

On average, women have a lower proportion of body water, so the same drink is less diluted. Research has also found that women, on average, break down less alcohol in the stomach before it reaches the blood. Together these mean women often reach a higher blood alcohol level from the same amount, even at the same weight.

**Can medications lower your alcohol tolerance?**

Yes. Sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioids, sedating antihistamines, some antidepressants, gabapentin, and muscle relaxants can all add to alcohol's sedating effect, and the combination can slow breathing. Some antibiotics, like metronidazole, cause a severe reaction with alcohol. Check the label and ask your pharmacist before drinking on any new medicine.

**Should I try to build up my alcohol tolerance?**

No. Building tolerance means drinking more often so your body adapts, but your organs are still exposed to the full amount of alcohol and you need more to feel the same effect. Higher tolerance is also an early warning sign doctors watch for. It's better to work with a low tolerance by eating first, pacing, and choosing lower-strength drinks.

**Does a low tolerance mean my liver is damaged?**

Not on its own. Most low tolerance comes from body size, occasional drinking, and the other everyday factors above. But a sudden drop combined with symptoms like yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, abdominal swelling, or easy bruising should be checked by a doctor.

**Can DHM increase my alcohol tolerance?**

There is no good evidence that DHM raises tolerance or lowers your blood alcohol level in a way you can rely on, and it doesn't make it safe to drive. Animal studies suggest it may affect how the brain responds to alcohol and how alcohol is cleared, but human research is limited. Food, pacing, and checking your medications matter far more.
